paragraphs.text: Section 1: Introduction to Linux
Open Source Operating System that is widely used and provide following features
Reliable
Free of Cost (Open-Source)
Software Management
Security
Performance
Freedom
Customization
Section 3: Understand & Use of Essential Tools
Terminal

The terminal allows the user to perform different system operations using the command line interface. The terminal follows this format: username@machine_name Directory $/#. ~ marks the home directory of logged in users. $ marks non-root user and # marks the root user
$ date -> displays current date & time
$ man command -> manual page of a command listing format and acceptable parameters
$ uptime -> shows uptime of the system along with logged in user
$ who -> display the details of logged in users
$ pwd -> shows current working directory
Linux File System Hierarchy
/ -> root directory; root of the file system
/usr -> Installed applications on the system, shared libraries
/usr/bin -> Binary files/Commands used by end users on the linux system (system wide binaries) e.g. cd, mv, etc.
/usr/sbin -> Binary files/ Commands only used by the administrator on the system directory
/usr/local -> Path Installed applications
/usr/tmp
/etc -> Contains configuration files of the system and applications
/var -> Files whose size is expected to increase by time such log files; Continuously changing files
/var/tmp -> same as /tmp but the files gets deleted after 30 days
/home -> stores home directory of each user; when a user is created, a directory with the username of the user is created inside this directory
/root -> home directory of the root user
/tmp -> temporary files used by the system or applications; these files get deleted after 10 days automatically
/dev -> has all devices files used by system to access the hardware such as hard disk
/boot -> contains boot loader files and kernels
/bin -> contains executable files that are part of the core operating system
/usr/share/doc -> documentation of applications on the system
File & Directories
$ touch -> Creates empty files on the path specified
$ touch file.txt -> creates a file with name “file.txt”
can also be used to create multiple files in a single by providing space separated path to each file name or comma separated list in side curly brackets ({file1.txt,file2.txt })
$ mkdir -> used to create empty directory
$ mkdir test -> creates a directory with name “test”
can also be used to create multiple files in a single by providing space separated path to each file name
use mkdir -p to create nested directories e.g. mkdir -p /dir1/dir2 will create a dir1 and dir2 inside dir1
Linux Shell Basics
$ whoami -> logged in user
$ hostname -> Machine Name
$ pwd -> current working directory
$ clear -> clears screen
$ ls -> shows files and directories
$ ls -l -> Long Listing Format  (shows more information about the files)
$ ls -a -> list all files and directories along with hidden files & directores (starting with .)
$ cd -> move between directories;
$ cd /path/to/directory
Can use relative or absolute path to directory to change the current working directory
$ cd .. -> moves to parent of current directory
$ cd -> moves to home directory of logged in user
File Management (copy, move, delete, rename)
$ cp source destination -> copies source content to destination
can be used to copy multiple files in a single command by specifying a list of source files separated by space followed by a destination
$ cp -v -> shows verbose
$ cp -r -> to copy directories
$ mv source destination -> moves source content to destination
can be used to move multiple files in a single command by specifying a list of source files separated by space followed by a destination
$ mv -v -> shows verbose
can also be used to rename a single file
$ rm file_path -> remove/delete files
$ rm -r -> delete directories
$ rmdir -> delete empty directories
Linux Man Pages
$ man x resource -> display manual page of the resource belonging to section x
man -k str -> search str across all manual pages and list all findings
Navigating through man page
Pg up -> Above page
Pg down -> next page
d -> next half page
u -> previous half page
Use / to search
G -> end of page
G -> start of page
N-> next finding
$ pinfo -> Similar to man pages but list more information regarding the resource
$ rpm -qd app -> find documentation of the application of the system
$ ssh user@machine -> connect to a remote machine at ip of machine with username “user”
If you don’t provide user, ssh will use the name of currently logged in user
I/O Redirection
> : Output redirect operator
ls > test.txt
Use >> to append the output to existing file
Prepend 1 for output and 2 for for error and & for both
< : Input redirect operator
Pipe ( | ) -> takes output from previous command and pass to next command
$ tee -> read from standard input and write to standard output and files
VI Editor
Command line text editor for Linux system
Three modes
Command Mode
Can’t type text
Executing commands such as copy, paste, del
Press i -> to go to insert mode
n yy -> to copy n lines
dd -> remove the current line
Shift+p -> past copied lines
cw -> replace current word
cc  -> delete content of the line
Insert Mode
Type text into the file
Press Esc to go to command mode
Last line mode
In command mode, type : to enter in last line mode
Archiving Files in Linux
$ tar -> archive files in linux
$ tar -cvf archive_name list of files -> to archive files
$ tar -cvf archive_name name of directory -> archive directories
$ tar -zcvf archive_name content -> archive files then compress it
$ tar -jcvf archive_name content -> archive files then compress it using bzip2
$ tar -tf archive_name -> list all files inside archive
$ tar -xvf archive_name -> extract contents of an archive
Compressing Files in Linux
$ gzip   file -> compress files
$ gunzip   file -> uncompress files
$ bzip2   file -> compress files
$ bunzip2   file -> uncompress files
$ xzip   file -> compress files
Hard & Soft Links
Hard Link
A pointer to the Inode of the file
$ ln file_path file_link_to_create -> create a hard link for the at the specified path
Both link and file have same inode number
Any modifications to the hard link also updates the file
Deleting original files will not affect the hard links created
Hard links can be used as backups
Soft Links
A pointer to the file
$ ln -s file_path file_link_to_create -> create a hard link for the at the specified path
Different Inode numbers for link and file
Deleting original files will affect the soft links created
Finding Files
$ locate search_key -> locate any file that contains search key in it name
Gives the result from locate database which stores filename and path
use -i flag for case-insensitive search e.g. $ locate -i search_key
Use -n to limit number of search results e.g.   $ locate -n 3 search_key
$ find path search_options  -> search files with specified search option inside the given path
-name for case-sensitive search
-iname for case-insensitive search
-group group_name for files owned by a group
-user user_name for files owned by user
-uid for files owned by a user
-gid for files owned by a group
-perm 000 for files with specific permissions
-size for files with specific size
-mmin -x for files modified within last x minutes
-mmin x for files modified x minutes ag
-mmin +x for files modifiedbefore last x minutes
-type {f|d|l} for searching on basis of file types
-links +x for files with hard links  (>= x hard links)
-type l searches for soft links
-type b searches for all block devices
Section 4: Linux System Administration (Chapter 1)
Local Users & Local Groups
$ id uname -> List group info of a user
$ ps -> list running process
$ ps au -> list user associated with the processes
/etc/passwd
Store information about local users in the system
Each line contains the information related to a user
Each line consists of seven fields separated by a colon (:) from left to right:
username
Initially password information was stored here but now stored in /etc/shadow file
User id
User’s primary group ID
User’s Name
Path to user’s home directory
Default Shell for the user (also shows if the user has access to shell or not)
/etc/group
Store information about local groups in the system
Each line contains the information related to a user
Each line consists of four fields separated by a colon (:) from left to right:
Group name
Second field is for password (not used)
Group id
Users that are members of the group
/etc/login.defs
Contains default configuration for adding a new user
Modify this file to update default configurations of the users created in future
Updating this file does not affect the already created users.
$ useradd uname -> to create a user in the system
$ passwd -> set a password for a user or update existing one
$ userdel uname -> remove a user from a system
Use -r flag to remove home directory & mail spool
$ groupadd name -> add a group with the specified name
$ groupdel name -> delete a group with specified name
Gaining Root Privileges
su or su - -> login as root
/etc/sudoers -> sudoers file containing root level permission for not root users
$ visudo -> Open sudoers file
Sudo -> can be used to run commands with root privileges if you are allowed to run in /ter/sudoers file or added in the wheel/sudo group
User Management
$ usermod -> update user details in the system
-g for changing primary group for user i.e. -g g_name u_name
-aG for append user to another group i.e.
$  groupmod -> modify an existing group
-n for renaming i.e. -n new_name old_name
-g for change group id i.e. -g new_id name
/etc/shadow
Stores users password information
Have 9 colon separated fields
Username
Encrypted Password
Days since last password change
Minimum number of days before a passwd must be changed
Maximum number of days before a passwd must be changed
Warning in number of Days before a password expires
Number of days account remains active after password expiration
Account Expiration Date in number of days
Reserved for future use
$  chage -> aging information about a user
-l  username -> lists the information
-d x username -> set number of days after which passwords expires, 0 forces immediate change of password
-M x username -> maximum number of days b/w password change
-m x username -> minimum number of days b/w password change
-E YYYY-MM-DD username -> set expiration date of the user
Configure a System to use Existing Auth Service
Packages required
authconfig-gtk
sssd
Krb5-workstation
Use $ authconfig-gtk to launch the LDAP config
Once configured, run $ getent passwd uname to verify successful connection
Us su to login as the LDAP user
Permission Notations

File/Directory permissions are represent as * --- --- --- where * represent the type of file and each group of three - represent permissions for users,group and others. E.g. d rwx r-x r-x represent a directory with read, write, execute permissions for user, & read and execute permissions for  group & others
The type bit value can have one of the three values:
- for regular files,
d for for directory
l for link
$ chown -> change ownership of files or directories
$ chown :newgroup file -> change group of file
$ chgrp -> change group of file
$ chmod -> chane file permissions
Numeric method -> represent permission in form of 3 octal number for user, group and other respectively
Symbolic Method -> use symbol to update permissions
u for users, g for group, o for others, a for all
r for read, w for write, x for execute,
use  + to add permissions and - to remove permissions
E.g. chmod u+x filename
Special Permission
Setuid
If enabled, let other processes/user run a file with permissions of the owner of the file .e.g. passwd
chmod u+s filename -> set setuid  bit
Setgid
If enabled on directory, all file inside that directory will have group of the directory as group value.
Chmod g+s -> set setgid  bit
Sticky Bit
Prevent deletion of file except from owner/root user
Chmod o+t -> set sticky bit
Umask
Used to set default permissions for new created directories
Files will have same permissions as directories excluding the execute permissions
Stored in .bashrc file located under home directory
Default umask is stored in /etc/profile file
Section 5: Linux System Administration (Chapter 2)
Monitoring running  processes
$ ps -> list running processes
Shows process id, terminal, elapsed time, and cmd name
$ ps aux -> provides more detailed information consisting of 11 columns
USER -> used related to process
PID -> Process ID
%CPU -> CPU utilization of process in percentage
%MEM -> Memory utilization of process in percentage
VSZ (Virtual Set Size) -> how much memory a process has available for its execution
RSS (Resident Set Size) -> Memory currently used by  a process
TTY -> Terminal
STAT -> Process State. Represented as a sequence of letters
First character indicates the state of the process
D -> uninterruptible sleep
R-> Running
S -> Interruptible sleep
Z -> Defunct (Zombie)
Second character shows additional information
W -> no resident page in memory
< -> high priority
N -> low priority
L -> has pages locked in memory
START -> Start time of the process
TIME -> How long the process has been running
COMMAND -> Name of the process
$ ps -ef ->  shows PPID along with other information
$ ps lax -> shows Flags (F), Nice Value (NI), Priority (PI) along with other information
Running Process in Background
To run a process in background, append a & at the end of the command
$ jobs -> list background processes
$ fg job_number -> bring a  background job to foreground
Press Ctrl+z to send a process to background
$ bg job_number -> start a background stopped process
$ kil %job_number -> terminated a background process
Terminate Running Process using kill & pkill
$ kill -SIGNAL PID or %JOBID -> using to terminate a running process with a specified signal
If you don’t pass any signal, the default (SIGTERM) (15)  is used
SIGKILL (9) -> terminates the process immediately without cleanup
$ pkill -> kill all the processes realted to a sevice
$ uptime -> list uptime, load on processor
/proc/cpuinfo  -> contains information related to CPU
$ top -> real-time information of memory
-d n -> refresh after evrey n seconds
Listing unit files Systemctl
$ systemctl -> manage services running on the system
$ systemctl  -t help list all the units types
$ systemctl status service_name -> status of a service
enabled service running on boot
$ systemctl –type=<type e.g.service> -> list all units of type service
$ systemctl is-active <service> -> check whether a service is active or not
$ systemctl is-enabled <service> -> check whether a service is enabled or not
$ systemctl list-units --type=service -> list all active services
$ systemctl list-units --type=service --all -> list all active and inactive services
$ systemctl list-unit-files --type=service -> list all unit files along with their status
$ systemctl --failed --type=service -> list all failed services along with their status
$ systemctl start service_name -> start a stopped service
$ systemctl stop service_name -> stop a running service
$ systemctl reload service_name -> reload configurations of the service with restarting it
$ systemctl enable service_name -> enable service to start on boot
$ systemctl disable service_name -> disable service to start on boot
$ systemctl mask service_name -> prevent anyone from starting a service
$ systemctl unmask service_name -> unmask a service
System Log Files
/var/log -> contains system log files
$ tail -n x filename -> list last x number lines from  the file
If n is not specified, 10 lines are displayed
$ head -n x filename -> list first x number lines from  the file
If n is not specified, 10 lines are displayed
lastlog file can’t be read by head, tail or less since it is a binary file
To view its content, use $ lastlog command
syslog -> protocol responsible for logging events in log files
Logfile rotation
the logfile is renamed with an appended date of rotation; a new log file is created in which system dumps log; this is done  using logrotate utility
System keeps the rotated log files for four weeks; after which they are deleted
syslog is handled by two services
rsyslog
Responsible for collecting data from different parts of the linux system and routing it to an appropriate log file
Data can also be routed to another linux server
/etc/rsyslog.conf -> main config file for rsyslog service
Message Priorities
emerg -> System is unusable
alert -> action must be taken immediately
crit -> Critical Condition
err -> error with the service
warning -> warning message
notice -> attention required
info -> Info message
debug -> debug info from the service
Different type of facilities in Linux
auth or authpriv -> message coming from authorization or security related events
kern -> kernel message
mail -> message from mail subsystem
cron -> Chrome Daemon Messages
daemon -> daemon messages
news -> network subsystem messages
lpr -> printing related messages
user -> user programs messages
Local0 to local7 -> reserved for local use
/etc/rsyslod.d/ -> custom config files can be added inside this directory
Format priority(* for all, none to for zero).facility /path/to/store/logs
$ logger -> can be used to generate log messages
SystemD journal  (journald)
System service for collecting and storing log data
/run/log/jornal/*/system.journal file
Clears logs each time you reboot the system
$ journalctl ->Displays logfiles in system.journal
$ journalctl -n x -> display last x line from journald log file; defaults to 10
$ journalctl -p x -> display all messages with priority xfrom journald log file
$ journalctl -f  -> similar to tail -n; monitor jornald log file and display updates
$ journalctl --since x -> display all messages written since time x
$ journalctl --since “YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS” --until “YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS”- -> display all messages written between two date
$ journalctl _SYSTEMD_UNIT=x -> display all messages of system unit x
Saving System Logs on File System
Journald has a built in logrotation that keeps data for a month
/etc/systemd/journald.conf -> configuration file for systemd journal
Create a directory @ /var/log/journal
Change the owner group of the directory to root and systemd-journal respectively
Change the directory permissions to 2755
Reboot the system
Successful shutdown & reboot a system
Commands that can be used to reboot the system
$ reboot
$ shutdown -r
$ Init 6
$ telinit
$ systemctl reboot
Command to Shutdown the system
$ shutdown
Broadcasts a message to all users that the system is going to shutdown
$ shutdown -h HH:MM -> schedule system poweroff
$ halt
$ systemctl halt
$ init 0
$ telinit 0
$ poweroff
$ systemctl poweroff
Boot into Different Targets
/usr/lib/systemd/system
Target -> different states that your system can boot into
Systemd -> system management daemon
Older version use init
$ systemctl get-default -> get default target
$ systemctl list-dependencies target_name -> list of services dependent on the target
$ systemctl isolate target_name -> switch to a different target
$ systemctl set-default target_name -> set default target
Adjust Process Priority with renice
$ nice -n x command -> run a process with a specified nice value x
$ renice -n x PID -> change the nice value of a running process with PID
Section 6: Linux System Administration (Chapter 3)
Linux File System
$ df -> display partitions and their usage
$ df -h -> display partitions and their usage in readable format
tmpfs  -> temporary file system; uses local memory for file system reads and writes
$ du -> works similarly like df but run on directories
$du -ah -> for extra details and human readable format
Mounting File System
$ blkid  -> list the UUID of the file systems on the system
$ mount /dev/dev_id  /mounting/point ->mount a partition on the specided path
$ mount UUID=”UUID of device”  /mounting/point ->mount a partition on the specided path
$mount -a -> mount all the file systems listed in /etc/fstab/ file
$  umount /mounting/point ->  unmount a device
$ lsof /mounting/point -> list processes using the device
$ fdisk -l  -> list all the partitions along with their details
$ parted -> utility for managing disk and partitions in file system
$ fdisk /dev/<dev> -> create partition inside a disk
$ mkfs -t <target_file_system> /dev/<dev_id> -> format a a partition with a specific file system
$ fsck.<file system> /dev/<dev_id> -> check and repair one or more linux file systems
$ dumpe2fs /dev/<dev_id> -> display information about a partition
$ xfs_info  /dev/<dev_id> -> list information about xfs file system
$ xfs_repair  /dev/<dev_id> -> heck and repair xfs file system
CIFS & NFS
Both Network File System (NFS) & Common Internet File System (CIFS) are file sharing protocols that allows you to configure a server to be a file sharing system across the network
NFS is used to share file system among the Linux Machines.
CIFS is used when you want to share a file system among a mix of Linux and Windows Machine
NFS
Add hostname of your NFS Server in /etc/hosts
$ mount -t nfs hostname:/path/to/shared /mounting/point -> Mount an NFS Share
To make the mounting boot persistent, add an entry with /etc/fstab  file
Hostsname:/path/to/shared /mount/pint nfs4 default  0 0
CIFS
Add hostname of your NFS Server in /etc/hosts
To make the mounting boot persistent, add an entry with /etc/fstab  file
//Hostsname/shared /mount/pint cifs rw,user=uname,password=passwd  0 0
Logical Volumes
Use t in $ fdisk /dev/<dev_id> to change the disk to logical volume.
Type L to list all the possible values
$ pvcreate /dev/<dev_id> -> to create a physical volume
$ pvdisplay -> list physical volumes
$ vgcreate name /path/to/partition -> create a volume group
$ vgdisplay -> list all the Volume Groups
$ lvcreate -n name -L size <volumeGroupName> -> Create a logical volume with specified name and size
$ lvdisplay -> list logical volumes
$ pvmove /dev/<dev_id>  /dev/<dev_id> -> Move data from one physical volume to other
$ vgreduce vg_name /dev/<dev_id> -> remove a volume from a volume group
$ lvextend -L 7G /dev/vg_name/data -> extend the logical volume size
$ xfs_growfs /mt/pt -> reflect changed size of lv for xfs FS
$ resize  / -> reflect changed size of lv forEXT4  FS
Access Control List (ACL)
Gives you ability to add more flexible permission mechanism for your files system
Enabled by default in ext4 & XFS file systems
$ getfacl /path -> ACL of the Specified directory/file
$ setfacl -m u:uname:permission /path ->  to provide user permissions to a file/directory by updating ACL

$ setfacl -m d:u:uname:permission /path ->  to provide user permissions to a directory by updating ACL; also enabling files & directories within to inherit the Updated ACL; only for newly created directories
$ setfacl -R -m u:uname:permission /path -> updated the ACL of directory recursively
$ setfacl -m g:uname:permission /path ->  update ACL of the groups
$ getfacl /path | setfacl --set-file=- filename -> copy ACL of one file to another
Network Time Protocol (NTP)
NTP synchronizes the time on your system with a centralized NTP server
$ timedatectl -> list current time configuration
$ timedatectl list-timezones -> list all the time zones
$ timedatectl set-timezones <timezone> -> change the timezone of the of your system
/etc/ntpd.conf -> config file for ntp
$ ntpq -p -> list detailed time synch information
$ ntpstat -> list basic time synch information
$ ntpupdate host -> Update the NTP server
$ chrony

synchronize the system clock with NTP servers, reference clocks: (e.g. receiver), and manual input using wristwatch and keyboard. It  can also operate as an NTPv4 (RFC 5905) server and peer to provide a time service to other computers in the network
/etc/chrony.conf -> configuration file for chrony
Update this file with local NTP servers like allow X.X.X.X
$ chronyc source -v -> list NTP servers
$ chronyc check -> Check NTP Configuration
Network Configuration
$ ip addr -> list all the network devices to system
$ ip addr show <nic> -> show information about the specified NIC
$ ip -s link show <nic> -> show information about the performance of specified NIC
$ ip route -> list all the possible routes
$ ping host -> check connectivity with  a host
$ ping -cx host -> ping a host with x number of packets
$ tracepath host -> trace path of the packet as it travels from  source to destination
$ traceroute -T host -> trace path of the packet as it travels from  source to destination using TCP
/etc/services -> All well known services for standard ports are listed in this file
$ ss -ta -> list all the connection on a system; LISTENING
$ ss -ta -> list all the connection on a system; LISTENING, also lists port number
$ netstat -> similar to ss
$ nmcli -> cli utility to configure the network connection on your system
$  nmcli con show -> list all available connections on the system
$  nmcli con show --active -> list all active connections on the system
$  nmcli con show “con_name” -> list all information about the specified connection
$  nmcli dev status -> list all network devices along with their status
$  nmcli dev show “dev_name” -> list all information about the specified network device
$  nmcli con add con-name <name of connection> type ethernet  ifname <device name> -> add a new connection
$  nmcli con mod con-name <name of connection> <options> -> modify an existing connection
$  nmcli con up -> start an existing connection
Editing Network Config Files
/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts -> config files for each NIC
You can edit hese config files to modify setting for the specific NIC
$  nmcli con reload ->  to reload connection confg
$  nmcli con del “con_name”->  to delete a connection
Configure Hostname and Name Resolution
$ hostnamectl -> utility to manage hostname of the system
$ hostnamectl set-hostname <hostname> -> change hostname of system
/etc/hosts -> contains host to IP mapping for different host; system looks for host IP in this file first; If not found it goes to DNS server
Install & Update Software with yum
$ yum  -> package manager in Linux
$ yum list -> list all the installed packages
$ yum list “str”-> list all the installed packages matching a string sequence or regex
$ yum search “str”-> search all the available  packages matching a string sequence or regex
$ yum info “pkg_name”-> list information about a package
$ yum provides /path/to/file -> list packages that configures this specified file
$ yum install “pkg_name” -> install a specific package
$ yum update  -> update installed system packages
$ yum remove “pkg_name” -> remove a specific package
$ yum grouplist -> list all yum groups
$ yum group info “grp_info” -> list all info about a  yum group
$ yum group install “grp_info” -> install all packages inside a yum group
$ yum history -> history of actions on packages
/var/log/yum.log -> log file of the yum package manager
rpm package files -> package manager
$ rpm -q “pkg_name” -> display info the package specified
$ rpm -q -f /path/to/file -> list packages that configures6 this specified file
$ rpm -q -l “pkg_name” -> list all files installed by package
$ rpm -q -d “pkg_name” -> path of documentation file for the server
$ rpm -ivh  “repo_link” -> install a repo from the provided link
Task Scheduler
Linux enables you to run specific bash scripts/commands at specific time by use to at and cron
$ at <time string to execute commands> -> provide commands and press Ctrl+D to save the scheduled job
$ atq -> list all at jobs
$ atrm job_num -> remove a job
/etc/at.deny -> any username  inside at.deny won’t be allowed to use at command
/etc/at.allow -> any username  inside at.deny will be allowed to use at command
Both of the above two files are mutually exclusive i,e, only one exist at a time
Cron job -> schedule task to run periodically
$ crontab -> command used to manage cron jobs
/etc/crontab -> stores all the cron jobs
$ crontab -e -> open the crontab files
A cron jon entry 7 fields separated by space
Minutes (0-59)
Hour (0-23)
Month (1-12)
Day of Week (0-6) Sunday = 0
User
Command
$ crontab -l -> list all cron jobs
$ crontab -l -u uname-> list all cron jobs of a user
$ crontab -r -u uname->remove all cron jobs of a user
/etc/cron.deny -> any username  inside cron.deny won’t be allowed to use at command
/etc/cron.allow -> any username  inside cron.allow won’t be allowed to use at command
Both of the above two files are mutually exclusive i,e, only one exist at a time
/etc/cron.d -> directory for custom cron jobs; any files inside this directory will be read by the cron  and run
$ cron  misses the schedule if the system is powered off this limitation is overcome by anacron
$anacron -> doesn’t assume that your system is up and running 24/7; it executes job after the downtime
Uses timestamps associated with files to see when it was last run and comparing it with its cron entry, it runs the command if necessary
$anacron -n -> run all anacron jobs
/var/spool/anacron -> anacron stores timestamp in this file to compare for next execution
An anacron entry consists of four columns
Period In days
Delay In Minutes (time after which the command runs, after starting anacron)
job-identifier
command
Section 7: Linux System Administration (Chapter 4)
Key based SSH Authentication
$ ssh-keygen -> to generate pub/priv key pair
$ ssh-copy-id root@remoteServer -> copy the public key to remote server
$ ssh root@remoteServer -> connect to remote server
Disallow Root User Remote Login
/etc/ssh/sshd_config -> Main Configuration File for SSH
Update this file with PermitRootLogin parameter set to no to disable root user remote login
Update this file with PermitRootLogin parameter set to without-password to allow only ssh key
Update this file with PasswordAuthentication parameter set to no to allow only ssh key for non-root users
Copying Files Securely between Systems
$ scp  /path/to/source /user@IP:/path/to/destination -> copy local files to a remote server
$ scp  -r /path/to/source /user@IP:/path/to/destination -> copy local directories to a remote server

$ sftp

$ put filepath -> upload files to remote server

similar to scp but copies the changes only

Firewalld service

Zones
gives your more flexibility by adding rules to multiple zones

$ firewall-cmd --get-default-zones -> list default zone of firewall
$ firewall-cmd --list-all -> list firewall rules of the default zone

Introduction to SELinux (Security Enhanced Linux)
Add/.s another layer of security to the Linux
Limits access to files to prevent malicious attacks
Can prevent users from executing shell scripts inside their home directories
Uses booleans to make its policy more flexible
/etc/sysconfig/selinux -> config file for SELinux
SELinux operates in three modes
Enforcing -> policies enforced
Permissive -> prints warnig instead of enforcing
Disabled -> No SELinux policy
$ sestatus -> get current mode of SELinux
$ getenforce -> get current mode of SELinux
$ setenforce  mode -> set current mode of SELinux
SELinux has  three policies
Targeted -> targeted processes are protected
Minimum -> Only selected processes are protected
mls -> Multi-level security protection
Labels
Set in context
Every process has an associated context type
$ semanage fcontext -l -> list all possible contexts
Any file created within directory will inherit the context from its parent directory
$ restoercon file -> resture default context of file
$ semanage context -a -t httpd_system_content_t ‘/mysites(/.*)?’ -> change the context of all files with in  directory
$ restoercon -RV /mysites -> apply the updated contex of the files and directories
$ semanage context -d ‘/mysites(/.*)?’ ->  delete the context type
$ getsebool -a -> get SELinux boolean and their current value
$ semanage bool -l  ->get SELinux boolean and their current value with details
$ setsebool <boolean_feature> value(on/off) -> enable or disable an SELinux Boolean feature
$ setsebool <boolean_feature> value(on/off) -P -> enable or disable an SELinux Boolean feature with persistance
/var/log/audit/audit.log -> SE Linux Log Files
$ sealert /var/log/audit/audit.log -> View SE linux logs in a more readable format

Configuring Network Teaming
Network teaming provide the following benefits:
Network teaming ensures a high level of availability.
Multiple connections provide the best performance.
In the event of system hardware breakdown, it assures network continuity.
It allows traffic to be rerouted across networks
Package teamd is used ot configure network teams
$ nmcli con add type team con-name team0 ifname team0 config ‘{“runner”: {“name”: “activebackup”}}’ -> create a new masterteam connection
$ nmcli con add type team-slave con-name team0-slave0 ifname eth0 master team0 -> create a slave team connection
$ teamdctl team0 state ->  current state of connection team
$ pin6 -I interface_name IPv6 -> ping an IPv6
Firewall (Rich Rules)
Helps create complex firewall rules in a more easy to understand manner
$ firewall-cmd --add-rich-rule ‘rule family-ipv4 source address=x.x.x.x accept’
Create a rich rule
You can add --permanent to make the rule persistent
More info in -> $ man 5 firewalld.richlanguage
Configuring Network Address Translation (NAT)
Can be done by Masquerading or Port Forwarding
Masquerading
Used to forward traffic from internal network to public network through a configured server that acts like a router
$ firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-masquerade -> enable masquerading
$ firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --remove-masquerade -> disable masquerading
Port Forwarding
Forwards all traffic, destined to a specific port, to a different port on the local machine/external machine
For external Linux Machine, Masquerading needs to enabled before using the port forwarding
Command to add port forwarding rule
Configuring System as an iSCSI Target
iSCSI ->
Internet Small Computer Systems Interface
Network protocol that allows you put hard disks in a sandbox.
Consists of two Components i.e. Target & Client
Target
$ targetcli -> CLI interface to configure iSCSI target
> backstores/block create block1 /dev/sdc -> Create a block storage object
> iscsi/ create iqn.2017-03.com.ine:t2 -> create  qualified domain name for the target
> cd iscsi/iqn.2017-03.com.ine:t2/tpg1 -> open the block storage object
> luns/ create /backstores/block/block1 -> Create Logical Unit Nmbers
> acls/ create  iqn.2017-03.com.ine:client -> Create ACL for  client
> cd acls/iqn.2017-03.com.ine:client/
> set auth userid=lunuser
> set auth password=12345
Open ports in the firewall for your block storage
Start  the target service
Client
$ iscsi-initiator-utils -> package to configure iSCSI client on system
/etc/iscsi/ -> Configuration directory containing config files for iscsi
Update iscsid.conf with username and password of the target
Add initiatorname.conf containing fqdn of the block storage device
$ systemctl start iscsi -> start the iscsi service
$ isciadm --mode discovery --type sendtargets --portal X.X.X.X
Return fqdn of the iSCSI target
$ isciadm --mode node --targetname fqdn_of_iscsitarget --portal X.X.X.X --login
Connect to the iSCSI target
Kernel Runtime Parameters
/proc/sys/kernel -> contains all the kernel related information files
$ sysctl -a -> list all system parameters
$ sysctl -a | grep kernel -> list all kernel parameters
$ sysctl -w kernel.<parameter>=value -> change the value of the kernel parameter
$ echo “value” >  /proc/sys/kernel/<parameter> -> change the value of the kernel parameter
This method is not boot-persistent. For boot-persistent kernel changes, edit the /etc/sysctl.conf and add a line in the format kernel.<parameter>=value, and save it.
System Reports
$ iostat -> displays average CPU and the devices on the system
$ pidstat -> displays information about the current running processes
/etc/sysconfig/sysstat -> configuration file for sysstat
/var/log/sa -> directory for log files
